The estimation of interaction and quadratic effects in regression models with observed variables is a well-known procedure behavioral and social sciences [@aiken_west_1991; @rimpler_etall_2025; @olvera_astivia_etall_2025]. In that case, an interaction is commonly calculated by the product of certain predictors, whereas a quadratic term involves the product of a predictor with itself. This allows researchers to study, for example, the dependency that one variable may have on the level of another variable, given the functional form at hand [@mize_2019]. In a structural equation model (SEM) we usually have a regression function with latent variables (e.g., latent variable model or structural part) [@bollen_1989]. The "triviality" of estimating interaction and quadratic effects in this setting goes away because the scores (e.g., the subject-specific values) on the latent variables are, at the time of measurement, unobserved [@bollen_hoyle_2012].

Despite that, the possibility to estimate latent interaction and quadratic terms is important. Indeed, previous research suggests that quadratic and interaction effects may "mask" or distort each other when predictors are correlated, leading to incorrect conclusions if not estimated simultaneously [@belzak_interaction_2019; @ganzach_misleading_1997]. Second, researchers should not have their theoretical models constrained by technical limitations—if theory suggests nonlinear effects exist, appropriate methods should be available [@oberauer_lewandowsky_2019]. Moreover, SEM accounts for measurement error by partitioning indicator variance into latent factors and residual error, which is important because observed product terms are typically less reliable than their components [@fisicaro_lautenschlager_1992; @bohrnstedt_marwell_1978]. Additionally, while Marsh et al. (2012) highlighted that latent variable models may contribute to higher statistical power, this may not hold generally [@Fuller1987; @cham_etall_2012] and requires more nuanced investigation.

Hence, multiple frequentist-based methods have been proposed in recent years that reflect successive attempts to address specific limitations identified in previous methods [@kenny_judd_1984; @joreskog_yan_1996; @algina_moulder_2001; @klein_moosbrugger_2000; @klein_muthen_2007; @marsh_etall_2004; @bollen_1995; @wall_amemiya_gapi_2001; @wall_amemiya_2003; @wall_amemiya_2000; @mooijaart_bentler_2010; @mooijaart_satorra_2012; @boker_etall_2023; @kelava_etall_2014]. However, these approaches differ substantially in their practical accessibility and in the assumptions required for their estimators to maintain desirable properties [@kelava_brandt_2022]. Building on this, simulation studies have provided empirical evaluations of these methods' performance under multiple conditions [@marsh_etall_2004; @cham_etall_2012; @brandt_etall_2014; @brandt_etall_2020; @lonati_etall_2024]. With a few notable exceptions, most of these approaches follow a joint ("system-wide") estimation method, meaning all parameters are jointly estimated. Indeed, that is the case for the more widely available approaches: Latent Moderated Structural Equations (LMS), Quasi-Maximum Likelihood Estimation (QML), and Product indicator (PI) approaches (e.g., XWITH command in Mplus and *nlsem*, *semTools*, *modsem* packages in R).

In the PI approach, manifest products of linear indicators serve as indicators of latent nonlinear factors (interactions or quadratics) that enter the structural model [@kenny_judd_1984]. Early constrained specifications imposed algebraic relations tying PI measurement to the linear measurement model, securing identification but restricting models to assumptions often violated by the non-normality of indicator products [@kelava_etall_2011]. Subsequent approaches removed most constraints, where relevant to this article is the Unconstrained PI (UPI) [@marsh_etall_2004] that was also extended to models with both interaction and quadratic terms [@kelava_brandt_2009; @brandt_etall_2014; @kjell_etall_2024]. Research has also explored optimal strategies for constructing product indicators, including mean-centering, residual centering, and double mean centering [@marsh_etall_2004; @schoemann_jorgensen_2021; @kjell_etall_2024]. The LMS and QML address normality violations without creating measurement models for nonlinear terms [@klein_moosbrugger_2000; @kelava_nonlinear_2014]. Indeed, the LMS approximates non-normal distributions using mixtures of normals, applying the EM algorithm to numerically integrate weighted multivariate distributions [@klein_moosbrugger_2000; @kelava_brandt_2022]. The QML offers a computationally efficient alternative by replacing non-normal distributions with normal approximations preserving the same mean and variance, allowing estimation via a quasi log-likelihood with minimal efficiency loss [@klein_muthen_2007].

Apart from the system-wide estimation, multiple structural-after-measurement (SAM) approaches were proposed in the literature for estimating nonlinear effects [@ng_chan_2020; @wall_amemiya_2003; @wall_amemiya_2000; @cox_kelcey_2021]. These methods follow similarly to the standard practice when all variables are observed, using factor scores to form quadratic and interaction terms. However, factor scores retain measurement error, amplified in their products [@bohrnstedt_marwell_1978], which SAM methods explicitly account for in the structural model. Recently, @rosseel_etall_2025 proposed the *local* SAM (LSAM) for estimating latent interaction and quadratic effects. This approach is closely connected to the more general two-stage method of moments (2SMM) [@wall_amemiya_2000; @wall_amemiya_2003]. In @rosseel_etall_2025, a small simulation study was conducted to evaluate the LSAM approach, which was limited to examining bias and variability of point estimates under a small set of conditions. Therefore, the aim of this paper is to further extend their work by analyzing standard errors, coverage, type I error rate, and power.

A comprehensive LSAM evaluation requires comparing its performance against established methods under conditions testing their underlying assumptions. Different approaches rely on distinct distributional assumptions, and violation impacts vary considerably. Beyond distributional concerns, @rosseel_etall_2025 claimed LMS, QML, and UPI face "scalability" limitations as higher-order terms increase, though the extent remains unclear. This may explain why previous literature focused on elementary interaction models (EIM) [@jaccard_wan_1995], with few studies examining models with three or more nonlinear terms (e.g., Klein & Muthen, 2007; Brandt et al., 2014). In fact, little work has addressed the statistical models for multiple endogenous variables for LMS and QML [@jin_etall_2020; @wall_amemiya_2007], requiring specific programming modifications [@kjell_etall_2024]. To investigate these concerns, we conduct two simulation studies comparing LSAM with LMS, QML, and the (extended) UPI with double-mean centering, examining their performance across distributional, reliability, and sample size conditions. The second study uses a model with eight nonlinear terms to assess scalability concerns.

The rest of this paper is organized as follows. In the next section we present an overviews of the approaches, together with their distributional assumptions and performance implications. We then present the simulation design, computational details, and performance measures before reporting results and concluding with a general discussion.
